stem: What is the function of mitochondria?

options.rationale: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts.
Proteins are made on ribosomes.
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration.

options.content: Controlling the activities of the cell
options.rationale: The nucleus controls the cell's activities.

explanation: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy from nutrients such as glucose. Both plant and animal cells contain them.

stem: Which part of a cell controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell?

options.rationale: The cell wall is fully permeable: it lets almost everything through.
The partially permeable membrane controls what enters and leaves.
The nucleus controls the cell's activities, not what crosses its boundary.
Most chemical reactions happen in the cytoplasm.

explanation: The cell membrane is partially permeable, so it controls which substances enter and leave the cell. A plant cell wall is fully permeable.

stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but **not** in animal cells?

options.rationale: Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria.
Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus.
Both plant and animal cells have ribosomes.
Animal cells have no cell wall.

explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall (and a large permanent vacuole and, in green parts, chloroplasts). Animal cells have none of these. Both types have mitochondria, a nucleus and ribosomes.

stem: Which list contains **only** structures found in both plant cells and animal cells?

options.rationale: All four are present in both types of cell.
Animal cells have no cell wall.
Animal cells have no chloroplasts.

options.content: Cytoplasm, large permanent vacuole, nucleus, cell membrane
options.rationale: Animal cells have no large permanent vacuole.

explanation: Plant and animal cells both have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. The cell wall, chloroplasts and large permanent vacuole are found only in plant cells.

stem: Select **all** the structures found in a bacterial cell.

options.rationale: Bacteria have a cell wall (not made of cellulose).
Bacteria have no nucleus.
Bacteria make proteins on ribosomes.
The genetic material is a loop of DNA in the cytoplasm.
Bacteria have no mitochondria.
Many bacteria have small extra rings of DNA called plasmids.
Bacteria have no chloroplasts.

explanation: A bacterial cell has a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, a circular chromosome of DNA and often plasmids. It has no nucleus, no mitochondria and no chloroplasts.
hints: Bacteria are prokaryotes: which structure does 'pro-karyote' (before the nucleus) tell you is missing?

stem: Match each cell structure with its function.

right.content: Contains genetic material that controls the activities of the cell
Strengthens the cell and stops it bursting
Stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm

explanation: Nucleus: controls the cell; ribosome: makes proteins; chloroplast: photosynthesis; cell wall: strength and support; vacuole: stores cell sap. Releasing energy in respiration is the job of mitochondria.

stem: True or false: all plant cells contain chloroplasts.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Root cells and onion bulb cells receive no light and have no chloroplasts.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Only cells in the green, light-receiving parts of a plant have chloroplasts.

explanation: Chloroplasts are found only in cells of the green parts of a plant that receive light, such as leaf mesophyll cells. Root hair cells and the cells of an onion bulb have none.

stem: True or false: plant cells contain mitochondria.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. Plant cells respire all the time, so they need mitochondria as well as chloroplasts.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Plant cells carry out aerobic respiration, which happens in mitochondria.

explanation: Every plant cell respires day and night, so plant cells contain mitochondria. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; they do not replace mitochondria.

stem: Name the structure in a plant cell that contains cell sap.

rejected.feedback: The cytoplasm surrounds the vacuole; cell sap is inside the vacuole.
The nucleus contains the genetic material.

explanation: The large permanent vacuole contains cell sap, a solution of sugars and salts in water. When it is full, it presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall and keeps the cell firm.

stem: Name the small rings of DNA found in many bacterial cells, in addition to the main circular chromosome.

rejected.feedback: The main DNA is the circular chromosome; the small extra rings are plasmids.
Ribosomes make proteins; they are not rings of DNA.

explanation: Plasmids are small, circular pieces of DNA carrying a few extra genes, such as genes for antibiotic resistance. They are used in genetic engineering.

stem: Which of these cells has no nucleus?

options.rationale: Onion cells have a nucleus, which shows up when stained with iodine.
Bacteria are prokaryotes: their DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
Cheek cells have a nucleus near the centre.
Palisade cells have a nucleus.

explanation: Bacterial cells have no nucleus; their DNA is a circular chromosome lying in the cytoplasm. Plant and animal cells such as onion, cheek and palisade cells all have a nucleus.

stem: A cell has a cell wall, a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a loop of DNA, but no nucleus and no mitochondria. What type of cell is it?

options.rationale: Plant cells have a nucleus and mitochondria.
Animal cells have no cell wall, and they have a nucleus.
Fungal cells have a nucleus and mitochondria.
No nucleus, no mitochondria and a loop of DNA are the features of bacteria.

explanation: The absence of a nucleus and mitochondria, together with a loop of DNA in the cytoplasm, shows that this is a bacterial (prokaryotic) cell.
hints: Which kind of cell has DNA but no nucleus?

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Match each label with the name of the structure.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which **two** labelled structures would also be found in a cheek cell?

options.rationale: Cheek cells have no cell wall and no large permanent vacuole.
Animal cells have a cell membrane and a nucleus.
Cheek cells have no cell wall.
Cheek cells have no large permanent vacuole.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State the function of structure P.

points.description: Strengthens / supports the cell, keeps its shape and stops it bursting when it takes in water

parts.explanation: P is the cellulose cell wall. It strengthens the cell, keeps its shape and stops it bursting when water enters by osmosis.

explanation: The cell wall (P) is the outermost layer, with the membrane (Q) pressed against it. The large vacuole (R) fills most of the cell and the nucleus (S) lies in the thin layer of cytoplasm. A root hair cell is underground, so it has no chloroplasts. Animal cells such as cheek cells have only the membrane and the nucleus of these structures.
hints: Which layer is outermost in a plant cell: the wall or the membrane?
Which of the labelled structures does an animal cell have?

stem: Tatenda prepares a slide of onion epidermis. He peels a very thin layer from an onion, places it in a drop of iodine solution on a slide and lowers a coverslip onto it at an angle.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Why must the layer of onion be very thin?

options.content: So that light can pass through it
options.rationale: A light microscope needs light to pass through the specimen.

options.content: So that the iodine kills the cells quickly
options.rationale: The thickness is not chosen to kill cells.

options.content: So that the cells grow larger
options.rationale: The cells do not grow on the slide.

options.content: So that the slide does not break
options.rationale: A thick layer would not break the slide.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Why is the coverslip lowered at an angle?

options.content: To spread the iodine evenly over the slide
options.rationale: The angle is not used to spread the stain.
Air bubbles would hide the cells.

options.content: To make the cells lie in rows
options.rationale: The cells are already in rows.

options.content: To stop the cells from drying out
options.rationale: Drying is prevented by the liquid, not the angle.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What is the main reason for adding iodine solution?

options.content: To test the cells for protein
options.rationale: Iodine solution tests for starch, not protein.

options.content: To kill bacteria on the slide
options.rationale: Iodine is used here as a stain.

options.content: To stain the cells so that structures such as the nucleus can be seen clearly
options.rationale: Unstained onion cells are almost transparent.

options.content: To provide the cells with food
options.rationale: The cells are not being kept alive for long.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State **two** ways in which the onion cells Tatenda sees will differ from cheek cells stained with methylene blue.

points.description: Onion cells have a cell wall; cheek cells do not
Onion cells have a regular / brick-like shape (cheek cells irregular) / a large vacuole (cheek cells none) / nucleus at the edge (cheek cells near the centre)

parts.explanation: The onion cells have a cell wall and a large vacuole and are regular, brick-shaped cells in rows, with the nucleus at the edge. The cheek cells have no wall and no large vacuole, are irregular in shape and have the nucleus near the centre.

explanation: Thin specimens let light through, a coverslip lowered at an angle avoids air bubbles, and stains make structures visible. Onion cells show plant features (wall, large vacuole, regular shape); cheek cells do not.
hints: How does a light microscope form an image?

stem: Complete the sentences about cell structures.

payload.template: Most of the chemical reactions in a cell take place in the {{blank:a}}. Proteins are made on small structures called {{blank:b}}.

explanation: The cytoplasm is the jelly-like material where most of the cell's reactions happen. Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.

stem: Which statement about the cell wall of a plant cell is correct?

options.content: It is made of cellulose, is fully permeable, and stops the cell bursting when it takes in water.
options.rationale: The strong wall resists the pressure of the cell contents.

options.content: It is partially permeable and controls which substances enter the cell.
options.rationale: That describes the cell membrane.

options.content: It is made of protein and contains chlorophyll.
options.rationale: The wall is made of cellulose; chlorophyll is in chloroplasts.

options.content: It is also found around animal cells such as cheek cells.
options.rationale: Animal cells have no cell wall.

explanation: The plant cell wall is made of cellulose. It is fully permeable, so it does not control what enters, but it is strong: it gives the cell its shape and stops it bursting when water enters.
hints: Which layer of a plant cell is partially permeable: the wall or the membrane?

stem: Compare the structure of a palisade mesophyll cell from a leaf with the structure of a cheek cell. [4]

points.description: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus and mitochondria
The palisade cell has a cellulose cell wall; the cheek cell has none
The palisade cell has chloroplasts; the cheek cell has none
The palisade cell has a large permanent vacuole; the cheek cell has none (or only small temporary vacuoles)
The palisade cell has a regular shape; the cheek cell is irregular

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Both cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus and mitochondria. The palisade cell has a cellulose cell wall, but the cheek cell has no cell wall. The palisade cell contains many chloroplasts, while the cheek cell has none. The palisade cell has a large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, but the cheek cell has no large vacuole. Because of its wall, the palisade cell has a regular shape, whereas the cheek cell is irregular.
answerSpec.markingNotes: Any four points. Each difference must refer to both cells.

explanation: A comparison needs similarities and differences, each stated for both cells. The palisade cell is a plant cell with a wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole; the cheek cell is an animal cell with none of these.
hints: For each difference, say what each cell has.

stem: Where is most of the genetic material of a plant cell found?

options.content: In a loop of DNA in the cytoplasm
options.rationale: That is how bacteria store their DNA.
The nucleus contains the chromosomes, made of DNA.

options.content: In the cell sap of the vacuole
options.rationale: Cell sap contains sugars and salts, not genetic material.

options.content: In the cellulose of the cell wall
options.rationale: The wall is made of cellulose, not DNA.

explanation: In plant and animal cells the DNA is organised into chromosomes inside the nucleus. Bacteria, which have no nucleus, keep their DNA as a loop in the cytoplasm.

stem: The cells of an onion bulb are plant cells, but they have no chloroplasts. Which is the best explanation?

options.content: Onion is not a true plant.
options.rationale: Onions are flowering plants (monocotyledons).

options.content: The bulb grows underground, in the dark, so its cells do not photosynthesise.
options.rationale: Only cells in parts that receive light develop chloroplasts.

options.content: The chloroplasts are destroyed when the slide is made.
options.rationale: Making the slide does not remove chloroplasts.

options.content: Onion cells use mitochondria for photosynthesis instead.
options.rationale: Mitochondria carry out respiration, not photosynthesis.

explanation: An onion bulb is made of storage leaves that grow underground. With no light, the cells cannot photosynthesise and do not develop chloroplasts, but they still have a cell wall and a large vacuole.
hints: What do chloroplasts need in order to work?

stem: A student has three unlabelled slides. One contains plant cells, one animal cells and one bacteria. Explain how she could use a microscope to decide which slide is which. [5]

points.description: Bacteria are much smaller (about 1–5 μm), so they need the highest magnification and show few internal details
Bacteria have no nucleus (DNA not enclosed), whereas plant and animal cells have a visible nucleus
Plant cells have a cell wall, giving a regular shape; animal cells have no wall and are irregular
Plant cells have a large central vacuole (nucleus pushed to the edge); animal cells do not
Plant cells from green tissue have chloroplasts; animal cells never do
Use a stain (e.g. iodine or methylene blue) / start at low power, then high power, to see the nucleus and other structures

answerSpec.modelAnswer: First she should look at each slide at low power, then at high power, using a stain such as methylene blue to show up the nuclei. The bacteria will be tiny (about 1 to 5 micrometres), so she will only see them clearly at the highest magnification, and she will not see a nucleus in them. Both the plant and the animal cells will be much larger and each will have a visible nucleus. The plant cells will have a thick cell wall that gives them a regular, box-like shape, a large central vacuole that pushes the nucleus to the edge and, if they come from a green part, chloroplasts. The animal cells will have no cell wall, no large vacuole and no chloroplasts, and their shapes will be irregular.

explanation: Size and the presence of a nucleus separate bacteria from the other two; a cell wall, a large vacuole and chloroplasts separate plant cells from animal cells.
hints: Which visible structures does only a plant cell have?

stem: Which statement about new cells is correct?

options.content: New cells form from non-living material in the cytoplasm.
options.rationale: Cells never form from non-living material.

options.content: New cells are made only in plants, not in animals.
options.rationale: Both plants and animals make new cells for growth and repair.

options.content: New cells are produced only by the division of existing cells.
options.rationale: Every cell comes from the division of another cell.

options.content: New cells are made by ribosomes joining together.
options.rationale: Ribosomes make proteins; they do not form cells.

explanation: All new cells are produced when existing cells divide. This is how organisms grow, repair damaged tissue and reproduce.
hints: Think about how a single fertilised egg becomes a whole organism.
